projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert D. Farren was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Robert D. Farren. Mr. Farren served in the U.S. Army. He was a medic attached to the 177th Engineers Battalion. He served in Alaska and the Aleutian Islands and his highest rank was P5. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made in Mr. Farren's home in Painesville, Ohio on December 20, 2002. Bob was 78 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: In 1941 I was living at 43 Kerr Avenue in Painesville, Ohio, and I was still in high school. I graduated from high school in 1942.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, absolutely.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What are your memories of that day?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Just of the anger. I think basically the anger. I was -- I was a young man who was mad at the Japanese from day one, you know. So I think that's, that's basically -- to think that they had the audacity to attack our Pearl Harbor, and in fact, attempt to take over our country. That was a rather serious matter to me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, you were still in high school, but did you have any idea that perhaps war was imminent for America?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, I thought sure that once the Japs attacked, we had to go to war. There's no choice as far as I was concerned. You know, I knew we would be at war immediately.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't think I've asked anybody this, but was school canceled the next day?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. As I recall that was -- was that a Sunday?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The attack was on a Sunday and then the FDR speech was on Monday.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I don't actually know if we went to school Monday or not. I don't remember that for a fact. I remember that it was Sunday was Pearl Harbor Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember listening to FDR's speech?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yes, I do. Yes, I do, and I've heard it thousands of times since then, too. It was a very inspiring speech.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you graduated in June of '42, is that right?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: June of '42. And I went back -- I went to work. I -- I went to work at the diamond chemical plant here in Fairport Harbor, and I worked at the diamond until about February of '43. I enlisted in the Navy. I was going with a couple of friends of mine, and the three of us went to Cleveland. And apparently they had quotas at that time and only one of us went to naval training to Great Lakes. That was Bob O'Leary, and the other two of us, Bob Hesh and I came back home. In the meantime the draft board took over enlistments. So we went and volunteered for the next draft, which turned out it was probably the draft I would have gone into anyway. But we went up and volunteered for the next draft, so on the next call up we went. And as it turned again, Bob Hesh, my good friend, had a cyst, bone cyst, on his leg and they discovered that. He never went to the service at all. So he spent his time in California building ships, helping them build ships. So he did his share, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. So when were you inducted? When did you go in?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I think it was May 1st -- April 1st, April 1st, 1943. April 1st, April Fool's Day, I went in the Army.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you train?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Training Camp Grant, Illinois. It's just outside of Rockford, Illinois and 90 miles northwest of Chicago and I took my basic there. I took infantry basic. Actually, I took medical basic. We used no guns. But it was the same thing as infantry basic except for -- except for the guns. I was going to into the medical. So I had three months basic at Camp Grant, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any memorable incidents during your training?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, a lot of them, a lot of them. I remember the infiltration course very well where we crawled under the barbed wires and trace and bullets were going overhead and I was scared to death. But, you know, it's something you did because it was going to possibly save your life at a later time. And it was, it was rigorous. We had -- I remember, I remember one incident in particular. I never ate liver in my life. I despised liver. I wouldn't even look at it. We went on a 5-mile hike -- 25-mile hike. I take that back. We went on a 25-mile hike. We came back to camp, and they had liver for dinner that evening and I ate liver, and I've been eating liver ever since.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were so hungry it didn't matter.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Right. Other than that, basic was pretty much, you know, drill, drill, drill. And it was very rigorous and very exciting. Different. I've never been out of Ohio in my life except maybe to Pennsylvania. I think I went one time to Detroit. But other than that I had never been out of Ohio in my life, so it was a new experience for me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was it like being exposed to guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: It was -- it was an education. We had a lot of people from Kentucky. In fact, about half Ohio, half Kentucky in my barracks. And some of the people from Kentucky -- not all of them -- but there were people from Kentucky that were from backwoods of Kentucky that had very little education. And it was amazing to me that someone absolutely -- absolutely could not read or write. I didn't know that there was anybody in the world that could not read or write. But that's what -- that what's happens when you meet a lot of people. You meet different people from different parts of the world and everybody is different. But we were altogether at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was next then?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Then I took some I.Q. tests, of course, and I qualified for a couple of programs. I qualified for officer candidate school. I also qualified for a new program called Army specialized training program, ASTP, and it sounded very, very wonderful. We were going to -- the idea of whole program, we were going to take a year of college every three months. And it was cram courses, of course. So I opted to -- so I opted for the ASTP program, which I thought sounded very good. And then they shipped me to University of Illinois. That was called a star unit. I don't remember what S-T-A-R stood for, but it stood for something. It's where we took our tests, standard testing or something like that. To find out what part of the ASTP program you were qualified for. Well, I qualified for some engineering. So they sent me to college at North Central College in Naperville, Illinois, a very small town, about 5,000 people. We lived in a girls' dormitory. They moved the girls out and moved the soldiers in. And I was there for three months and went to school from like 8:00 o'clock in the morning until 8:00 o'clock at night. We had breaks, of course, for lunch and dinner. But we had study hall from 6:00 to 8:00 at night. And we had school from 8:00 o'clock until dinnertime in the evening. And that went on for three months and they transferred me to Bradley Polytechnical Institute in Peoria, Illinois, home of Jim Tony. (Laughter.) So, anyway, I was another three months and the program started expanding about that time. So I ended up going back to Camp Grant, Illinois for two more months of basic, which was kind of dull because I've already been through it once. From there I transferred to Fort Benjamin Harrison, Indiana, Billings General Hospital, where I took my medical surgical technician training. Worked in a hospital there and took my training as medical surgical technician. And after that went back to Camp Grant for another month of basic. From there I went to Camp Reynolds, Pennsylvania, which is a POR, port of reserve. That's where you're shipped out overseas from Camp Reynolds, Pennsylvania. I was there for -- I don't remember how long I was in Camp Reynolds, two or three months, maybe four months. I don't remember exactly. And most of my outfit shipped to Europe. At the time I was in the hospital when my outfit shipped out, so I didn't go with them to Europe. I stayed in Camp Reynolds until I got released from the hospital. I had -- it's not a pleasant thing to talk about, but I had trench mouth, which caused a lot of ulcers inside of my mouth and throat. I had some serious case of trench mouth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did that come on?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I don't know. It's brought on by drinking out of a dirty glass, or you know, of kissing the wrong girl, or something. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Don't kiss her again.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: But anyway to make a long story short, I got out of the hospital and the next shipment went to Alaska. So I went to Alaska. I got on a train from Camp Grant, Pennsylvania, on a train for five days and five nights. We had sleeper cars and we had porters, believe it or not. Actually, made up our bunks. But we had to walk down to the mess car to get out food, and we stopped twice a day for calisthenics along the way, across the Canadian border at Great Falls, Montana, went right up on through the heart of Jasper National Park, which is gorgeous, gorgeous country, to a place called Prince Rupert, Canada. And after a short stay in Prince Rupert, in a matter of days we got on the ship and we went to Whittier, Alaska. We got off the ship there, and we got on a train and went to Anchorage, Alaska. And I was in Anchorage for four months during the -- during the winter. It got down to 28 degrees below zero during the winter months, and our days were about five hours long, maybe six. And the sun would come about 11:00 and go down about 4:00. So we had very short days while we're there. But that part of Alaska is actually a lot of farming country. That's the lower part of Alaska, and I -- I was surprised to realize that. So I worked in a medical aid station, attached to the 177th Engineer Construction Battalion. Well, apparently the docks blew away on a little island called Shemya down in Aleutian Islands. Lot of storms down there, a lot of wind. So they needed somebody to build docks. So they shipped 177th Engineers down to Shemya to build docks. Well, we couldn't dock at Shemya because there were no docks. They both blew away, so we docked at Attu after a stop in Dutch Harbor, a stop in Kiska. We docked at Attu. And we were on Attu for nine days and we lived in tents for nine days. They had wooden floors, wooden platform floors. They had a potbelly stove in the middle of the room and four bunks in each tent, and it was very cold. The Japs had been there. The Japanese had attempted to invade the United States through Attu and Kiska. And the Japs had been there, but fortunately by the time I got there, fortunately from my standpoint, the war up there was over. The Japs had been ousted. And I did see some Japanese graves as a result from that battle. But to get back to our tents on Attu, these potbelly stoves, you stoke them up at night. We had to dig coal out of the ice and snow. They had a coal pile and we had to go down and dig your own coal. Then you'd stoke the stove up at night and we slept on cots and sleeping bags. Of course, when you go to sleep, the stove would be red hot, and you'd be toasty. So you'd unzip the sleeping bag and throw it open. You wake about 2:00 o'clock in the morning and the stove is out and it's cold in there. So it was kind of interesting there, and then we got on -- we got on planes and we flew to Shemya to build the docks. And I was stationed on the Island of Shemya, which is two miles wide and four miles long. And the only island in the Aleutians that doesn't have mountains, so it was all air base, it was all runway. We had a huge, long runway there. And so I was stationed on Shemya for 14 months. And it was very, very dull and drab. In fact, when we were rotating they had, they had a three-year rotation period. I think it was maybe two-year rotation period. But after you've been up there are two years, they were supposed to send you back to the United States. And I remember Eleanor Roosevelt one time visiting the Aleutian Islands and said, "Anybody that was up there for two years wasn't fit to go back to the United States." I don't know if that's a fact or not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why is that?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Well, it was so dismal, and like I was on the island with 10,000 men, and there were four women on there. We had four Red Cross girls and four nurses on the entire Long Island. So it was kind of lonesome, too, you know. But anyway I worked in a -- worked in an aid station there for a long time and eventually something happened that the aid station was closing up, and I went to work at a station hospital. And I worked in a station hospital the last few months I was there, and then it was time to come home. The war ended.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when you arrived in Alaska, this would be the winter of '44, '45?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So probably November, December '44 is when you got there?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Right, right, right. November, November of '44, I went to Alaska. And interesting thing about the 14 months I was on Shemya during the year of 1945, we had five days of sunshine. That's all the entire year, and we treated several cases of sunburn. (Laughter.) Because when the sun would come out, the guys would just go out and lay in there until they burned to a crisp. You know, I had a lot of interesting things happen there. I saw a lot of tragic things. I saw a lot of great things. I've loved airplanes ever since I was a kid, so it was fantastic to be that close to an air base and be able to see the airplanes, except they bombed the Creole Islands from Shemya almost daily, with B-24s. They're called flying boxcars. And I lived about probably, I don't know, maybe a quarter of a mile from the end of the runway and off to one side. That's where our hut was, and our huts were buried, more or less buried in the sand. They were dugged out, so that all the wind would go over the top because the wind -- the wind was so strong there. When you go up the hill, the sand blowing in your face would sting your face. And it was, it was cold, but not always real, real cold because of the Japanese currents that go by there. But anyway, these B-24s would be coming back from these bombing rounds and the island's fogged in, so they'd be a little off course. And when they'd actually visualize the runway, maybe three, four hundred feet off the ground, so they'd rev up all four of them engines right over my hut sometimes to try to get back on course. I was sure one day one of those B-24s would land on me. And when I first went up there, they had B-40 fighter planes. That's early in war. We had B-38s towards the end, and the last -- very, very near the end of war the first B-29s came in there because that's the northern route to Tokyo through the Aleutian Islands. That's why that runway was so important. And it was the only island up there that could land a plane that large, too. So.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now the B-24s were bombing, were there still Japanese?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. It was half Japanese, half Russian on the Creole Islands.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So there were still Japanese troops there until in the end of the war?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Right, right, right. Yeah, that was -- you know, I don't know how long it continued that. When I moved on to the station hospital, I kind of lost track of that. That was a whole different situation. But we had -- like I said, our huts were buried below the surface. Actually, they were dug into a trench and they sat in there. When I was in the hospital, we had one front door from the hut that went into a corridor that led to the hospital, and so we had no trouble there. But we tried to open the back door one morning, and it was all just solid snow. We were buried in the snow. The whole hut was buried in the snow. So and because I was in the station hospital, I got to know the four nurses that were up there. (Laughter.) So I had somebody to talk to anyway besides 10,000 other guys.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your specific job in the hospital?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I was -- well, like I said I was a medical surgical technician. I did just whatever they told me to do. I didn't do anything, you know, I didn't assist in surgery in great ways. But I had tended to surgical patients. I did bandaging. I carried bedpans. Whatever needed to be done, that's what I did. I was a bedpan commando. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now you mentioned the tragic things. With that much, especially the weather, was there a problem with depression?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I didn't have any problem with depression. I know that was there was a guy in our barracks that did. He'd almost drive you nuts. He'd talk about home all the time. I mean he was -- he was obsessed with idea of getting home. He did. He got home a lot earlier than I did. They gave him a Section 8, and they sent him back home because he kind of went gaga over the fact that he was so far from home. But, you know, things like that happened and we had -- we had other people. There was, believe me, there was lot of drinking on that island. And a lot of drinking things that you shouldn't have been drinking, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: So, but it was an interesting. And I actually liked the Army. I liked the Army well enough, so if I hadn't been anywhere except the Aleutian Islands, I might have re-upped because I gave -- they offered me three more stripes if I'd stay there for another year. And I opted not to because I -- I really didn't -- that wasn't the best place in the world to be, and I had been there long enough I thought. I, you know, I drove ambulance, too. We had an ambulance when I was in the aid station. Didn't have a lot of use for the ambulance, but we used it once in a great while. So I learned how to -- I learned how to double clutch. Never double clutched before in my life, you know. When you shift gears, you double clutch the old Army vehicles. So I got an education. I got an education.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you do for entertainment? Did you get any shows up there or anything?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We had -- we had movies all the time. We didn't get any USO shows. I never -- I never saw a USO show, but we had movies all the time. And I had -- excuse me. I had a radio by my bedside and I had a record player. In fact, I bought that from a guy that was rotating. He offered to sell it to me for something like twenty-five dollars and I offered him ten. And he said no, it's twenty-five dollars. I offered him ten. And that went on until just before he shipped out, and he sold it to me for ten dollars. And I had a stack of records and I, you know. Anita O'Day was one of my all time favorites singers, still is, and she was at that time with the Gene Krupa Band. She sang with several other bands, but I had a lot of records and I enjoyed that. I wrote a lot of letters. I wrote a lot of people back home. I'd write almost weekly to my folks. And we had our -- we had out beer ration and we had parties every Saturday night, especially when I was in the station hospital. I used to -- I still do play the accordion. I haven't played it for years. But I got an accordion from special services and when I was in Alaska -- no. I was in the Aleutian Islands, we had a guy in our hut that played the guitar. And he and I used to play the accordion and guitar together. And then when we'd have these parties on Saturday night, I'd take my accordion and I'd play the accordion while we'd party it up. I won't tell you what we drank. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were some of your favorite songs? What were some of the names of some of records that you had? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: The records I had?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, Anita O'Day so many songs and "Drum Boogie."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: "Drum Boogie" that song really rides. I still like that when I hear it today, and she did a thing called "Hi Ho Trailus Boot Whip." You probably haven't heard that one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: But I still have her record here. I still have many of Anita O'Day's records here. And of course, I was -- the Mills Brothers were very popular. I liked some of the "Paper Doll," and oh, many of the songs Frank Sinatra sang were favorite, just wartime favorites. Liked them all. I just liked music.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever make up your own songs?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. No, I never did any songs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I hear occasional stories of soldiers making up their own lyrics to popular songs, that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of getting mail from home? You mentioned writing letters home. Packages, mail from home?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah, the Christmas packages I remember well. My mother used to send me cookies, of course, and things like that. And I remember around Christmastime how welcome they were, you know. I don't remember how I spent Christmas down in the Aleutian. I remember the Christmas I spent in Alaska. There was another boy from Painesville that was in another part of Anchorage from where I was, and we got together on Christmas and Christmas Eve and just spent the evening together and which was kind of nice and shared our packages from home. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have a lot of close buddies?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. I had -- yeah, I had a whole bunch of close buddies. The guys who partied on Saturday night, we became very close, you know. We -- there was a guy from California named Embry. I can't remember. Carl Embry, I think it was and I always wondered, you know, there's a girl that works in the zoo out there, San Diego Zoo that's been on television.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. Joan Embry.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Joan Embry, and I often wondered if she was related to the Embry that I was in the Aleutian Islands with. There was a guy named Joe Pisano from Brooklyn, New York. He and I became good buddies. There was a fellow named Carl Shurid. He was from Schenectady, New York, and I had been to see him since I came back from the service, but it's been a long time since I've seen him. And not a lot -- not a lot of lasting friendships because we all broke up and went our own way. But a lot of good memories from the people that I palled around with up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I came home in '46. I was discharged 0n April 1st, '46. Just about three years from the time I went in until the time I came out. It was three years exactly, if you figure I went in April 1st. I was sworn in April 1st, and I went -- came back on April 1st. I was -- I was high man, point man. You know, you get so many points. When you got so many points, you're eligible to go home. I had the opportunity to -- a ship came in that was going back to the States. I had the opportunity to take that ship back, or I could wait and they would fly me home next time a plane was available. Well, I decided not to wait and take a chance on a plane, so I took the ship and got out of there. I can't remember the name of the ship. It seems like it was the -- it was either the Carl Schur, that I went up on or it was the Carl Schurz. It was a Liberty ship that I came back on. And once I was -- once I was settled to come home, then I had no more duties. I just -- I just became high point man. I just sat and waited for them to get some kind of vehicle to take me home. And I can remember watching airplanes flying. I figured maybe that's my plane. But eventually I got on the ship and I came home. We came through Seattle, Washington, and we got on the -- got on a train in Seattle, Washington and went to Camp Atterbury in Indiana, and I was discharged from Camp Atterbury, Indiana. And I still have some of old -- some of my old uniform here. In fact, I wore some of it out to Pearl -- that's the Pearl Harbor I remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I remember. What was I going to ask you? I got sidetracked. What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got home?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: It was fantastic. You know, it was just great to see everybody again. I was 22 years old. I had been away for a good part of three years. Although, I did get home frequently when I was in the States, especially when I was stationed in Camp Reynolds, Pennsylvania, before I went overseas because I could hitchhike home from there if I could get a pass. And I did that several times. But it was just wonderful to be back. And then, of course, you had to decide what you wanted to do with your life at that point in time because I hadn't made no serious decisions. I had a job at the time and that I eventually went back to. I joined the 5220 Club, which everybody is familiar with. It was in the service, and I drew twenty dollars for three weeks, and I couldn't stand it any longer. I went back to work.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughter.) Were you bored?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You needed some activity?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I needed -- yeah, I needed to do something. I just couldn't, you know, walk down and sit out in the soda hut all day long. Although that was kind of nice, too. Then I wanted to just get ahead with my life. So then I -- then I had this G.I. bill to think about, and I thought about it, and I thought about doing this and I thought about and eventually I did nothing. I let my G.I. bill go to waste, which was kind of unfortunate. But, I don't know if you want to go anywhere past that or not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you know, I'm curious about -- backtracking a little bit. You were, you were on the home front for a year and a half before you went into service?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What are your memories of being on the home front, rationing that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Of course, I remember the fact that we could buy a carton of cigarettes for 50 cents at the PX. And I also remember -- (laughter) -- I don't know if I can tell you this or not, but I remember after I got back from the service, I was dating a girl from Lake Erie College and hosiery was very, very hard to get. So I got some silk hose, somehow or other, and I call up the college and I said, "If I give you two pair of silk hose, will you go to bed with me?" And she said, "Yes. Who is this?" (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But she said yes first. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That probably won't get on the air, I'm sure. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bet the Library of Congress likes those kind of stories.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. It was just nice to -- when I was in the -- when I was in the States I knocked around from pillar to post so much that I really didn't have any time to set down. Went to -- went to North Central College in Naperville, Illinois, and the town was very receptive to the soldiers being there. We marched in the streets, of course. They had a dance. They had all the girls, young girls in town go to this dance, and all the soldiers were there. And to get acquainted, they had each girl put a shoe on the middle of the floor and at any given time, everybody went out and grabbed a shoe, and it was like looking for Cinderella, and you went and found your girl. And then you became acquainted. And I got the shoe from a girl that I had an eye on. And we did date some while I was there. Then I moved on someplace else, and that was over. So I was never anyplace long enough to really establish anything. I was three months here, three months there, three months here, three months there, and so I moved around a lot. And I was a casual, so I had no rank. I wasn't attached to anything really. Congress finally gave me a stripe. Congress passed a law that anybody that had been in the Army for a year with a good record should automatically become PFC. So that's when I became PFC. Eventually I was a technician fifth grade. That's called a corporal with a crutch. That's what they called them back in that day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why is that?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Well, it's got a T underneath it. It's two stripes with a T underneath it, so they called that corporal with a crutch.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: My dad ended up with that too, but I never heard that term.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Well, that's what they call them. Anybody with a T underneath there, that was their crutch. That was it. I sent a lot of money home when I was overseas, you know, because I didn't have a lot of use for money. We didn't have any post theaters in the Aleutian Islands. We had movies in the mess hall. You could go down. But we had a post theater when I was in Alaska. You had to walk about a half a mile through the woods, and when it was 28 degrees below zero up there, and you walked through these woods, it was scary because the snow would crack open. But it was -- lived right across the street when I was in Alaska. Lived in a hut right across the street from the motor pool. And they had to keep their motors running almost day and night up there, so things wouldn't freeze up. So, you know, sometimes it was hard to sleep at night with all the motors running up there. We had a day room. When I was in Alaska, we had a day room with a pool table and ping-pong and all that stuff. And I played a lot of ping-pong. I played a lot of ping-pong when I got down to the Aleutian Islands and I became fairly good at ping-pong at that time. Because as long as you won, you kept a table. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experience in the Army, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That trip from Camp Reynolds, Pennsylvania stands in my mind probably as much as anything. That trip on the train through the Canadian Rockies through Jasper National Park. I wrote my mother and father a letter, five days long. I wrote something every day on that trip and I still have that letter. It's in my scrapbook over here. But of all the things that we saw and all the wonders of world that I had never seen anything like that before in my life. And of course, when I got up to Alaska, Alaska is beautiful. Mount McKinley was, you know, it was miles away but it was majestic. We'd wake up in the morning and see Mount McKinley. Those are -- I'd never seen mountains before. Those are the kinds of things the places that I went and many things I saw that I can't -- I can't bring them all to mind right now. I was -- I was just awe-inspired and I enjoyed being in the Army. I at the time was very upset because I didn't see any battles, I didn't get any scrimmages. I one time attempted to enlist in the paratroopers. They were getting ready for the invasion of Japan at that time, they were talking about it. And I, of course, was up in the Aleutian Islands, and they were calling infantry people and paratroopers for training to go in the invasion force. So I had offered to go back and take paratrooper training, not necessarily just to get out of the Aleutian Islands. I liked paratrooping. I liked parachute jumping. I made one parachute jumping in my life after I came back. But anyway, I thought I would like to get into the paratroopers, but they declared my speck number 409 essential to that theater of operations. So I stayed there, and it wasn't all bad.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news when they had dropped the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I can't remember that. I remember V-J Day and I remember V-E Day quite well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What are your memories of V-E and V-J Day?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Well, of course V-J, V-E day came while I was still in the Aleutian Islands. I think V-J -- when did V-J Day come?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: V-J Day would be summer of '45, August.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. That was just before I rotated back home. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, those were happy days. Those were days to remember. But I -- I -- nothing -- we didn't do anything out of the ordinary in those days. We didn't do anything. There was no fireworks or anything like that. We had jobs. We were still doing our jobs. But we were just happy that those things happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any concept of what the atomic bomb was?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. No, none whatsoever. I knew that they had been testing and I had seen, of course, pictures of mushroom clouds. But I had no idea that the amount of destruction that bomb could do. And I'm not sure -- I'm not sure everybody knew how much destruction there was. Maybe a few people. But I think there were a lot of people that didn't realize how much destruction that bomb was going to do. Only I think, you know, forgive me for not being humane, or something, but I think it's what ended the war with Japan. And I think it probably saved more lives than were lost in it. And of course, they were Japanese life. They weren't American life. But still that's -- we probably saved more Japanese life than -- than if the war had extended for a great length of time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah, I do. I remember the day FDR died. I don't remember when it was, but I remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was April of '45.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: And, you know, I admired Frank Delano Roosevelt, he had been my president since 1932, as I recall.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: And I thought -- I thought he was a great man and I think Harry Truman was a great man. I think, I was so happy that Harry Truman beat Dewey in that election. (Laughter.) You don't know. I liked Harry because he call a spade a spade, but Franklin Delano Roosevelt, I give him a lot of credit because I went through the Depression, and I know what he did to bring us out of the Depression, works programs. I don't know if he had anything to do with setting them up, but he was the guy that signed the papers that set them up. Yeah, I admired Franklin Roosevelt and I admired Harry Truman.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction from the guys when they heard about FDR's death?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, a lot of sadness, you know. He was a great man that led us a long way and inspired everybody, you know. Of course, in that day -- that day was -- those days were different. I think -- I don't know. Today I wonder if everybody feels the same way about their country as we did back then. Maybe it would if we got involved in a conflict like that. But somewhere there's some doubt in my mind if there's the dedication that there was back then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did anybody know anything about Harry Truman at that point?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. No, I didn't know. I knew he was the vice president. That's about it. And I just -- I just think he did a great job taking over like he did. And he was the one that decided to drop the bomb and end the conflict. Who knows what had happened if he hadn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember feeling anything in the early days of the war that we might not win?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. No, never, never entered my mind. No, we were going to win. No doubt in my mind and nobody was going to get in this country. I remember the Japanese invasion of the -- through Aleutian Islands. Nobody was getting to get -- we weren't -- nobody was going to get in this country. And I remember the balloons, the balloon bombs that they sent over.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that. Did any come over where you were?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. We never had a balloon bomb come over. They had midget submarines that came nearby and we captured a couple of midget submarines, but that was the only thing. We never -- I never actually saw any Japanese after I went into overseas. But.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So explain how the balloon bomb was supposed to work.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: It was just supposed to come over until the balloon burst and then the bomb was supposed to fall and do some damage. That was kind of a hit and miss situation. Just like Hitler with the -- with the one-pound phosphor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Phosphorus?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Bombs that you couldn't put out with water.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, right, right.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. You know, the idea of those bombs was that they would start a fire, and you wouldn't be able to put it out. Maybe it would cause a lot of problems. They were never very successful, but they tried a lot of different things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they -- did they send any balloon bombs over Alaska or did they try to get them to the West Coast?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: They tried to get them to the West Coast mainly. They wanted to do some damage to the United States. I also remember quite vividly when Jimmy Doolittle bombed them. I saw Jimmy Doolittle flying in 1932 air races in Cleveland. He flew a thing called a Gee Bee Special.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. I've seen those.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Flew that little airplane right there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I have a similar one to this. I have a yellow and blue one.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: So I was tickled pink that Jimmy Doolittle led that flight, B-25s off that carrier and bombed Tokyo. Although, I've got to give those guys a lot of credit because they didn't know -- because they knew they didn't have enough gasoline to get back anywhere for where they're going. So there were similar to the Japanese suicide bombers in some -- to some extent. But most of them had a -- had a chance to get someplace hopefully. So I thought that took a lot of guts.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there a feeling that we'd gotten them back for Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. That helped a great deal. Just being able to bomb Tokyo helped a great deal, you know. Built up our morale. Yeah. Really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I can't think of anything else. You know, there were so many things that happened and it was so long ago that it's hard to remember everything that happened there. I know that I was -- I was happy I went, and I'm happy I got out without any -- you know, if I had gone with my -- with my unit from Camp Reynolds, Pennsylvania to Europe who knows what would happen. Some of those -- some of those gentlemen took paratrooper training in England and jumped in the invasion, that I was stationed on in Camp Reynolds, Pennsylvania with. And who knows what would happen if I'd gone with that group, but I didn't. I went to Alaska. I wasn't too happy at that time about going to Alaska and the Aleutian Islands, but I survived.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And held the line. They didn't come in. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I didn't realize you were fire chief. Fire Chief of Painesville?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Painesville City.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's probably why that name is familiar to me.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. I've been retired for 21 years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you probably knew Al Howells?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, I knew Al well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He was my next door neighbor.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: You still live there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I'll be. When my first wife and I used to travel around a lot, whenever we go to conferences, International Association of Conferences, I can remember running around all Denver with Al and all over Salt Lake City -- and I'm trying to think of the place in Texas where they have the river walk, jazz. Anyway.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Dallas, Houston, San Antonio.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: San Antonio. San Antonio, yeah. We spent time. And then, you know, Al and I used to get together here a lot. In fact, I was thinking about Al the other day. There was something in the paper about this guy that murdered his two -- his parents, set the house on fire.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: He was looking to get some kind of early release or something like that. I was in Al Howells's office the day he walked in, the day after the murders to talk to Al about that situation. And Frank Steinford, was a friend of mine, was on the fire department. Frank called me the day it was -- it happened and told me it looked like it was not -- not just fire death.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Because fire deaths were kind of unusual around here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think I do remember that.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I can't remember the guy's name. But anyway.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, the Howells we lived next to them for 50 years.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. I liked Al. Al was a straight shooter.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. And Syd is still doing great.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. I got a card from Syd. Syd and I still exchange Christmas cards and I don't stop and see her as often as I should because we were good friends for a long time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: If you do stop and see her, when you go up the long driveway, I'm the house off to the left.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I'll be damned. I've been by your house many times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I've been by that driveway a lot of times. Al and used to play golf together and besides traveling together, we spent a lot of time together, and we've worked fires together, of course.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, sure.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Mutual aid fires. He's a great guy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's take a brief look at your scrapbook.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I kind of looked at those in passing. See if anything else comes up here.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Here's my patch from the -- from the Alaskan theater in here someplace, too. There.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, that's great.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's the North Star and a polar bear. But.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Christmas dinner. What was Christmas dinner?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: 1944, Christmas dinner. Turkey, noodle soup, Roast Young Tom Turkey, sage dressing, whipped potatoes with gravy, butter, asparagus, chips, green beans with bacon, hot buttered rolls, cherry and pumpkin pie, plumb pudding, rum sauce, cranberry sauce, fruitcake, assorted nuts, olives, popcorn, coffee, chocolate milk, lemonade, and favors.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's a great meal, uh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. What are favors?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That was a good question. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It says favors.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I don't know. See, this is a -- this is when I went with George Kleinfeld. He's the kid from Painesville.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Went down to the main base to have Christmas dinner with George Kleinfeld. That's the guy from Painesville.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you keeping this scrapbook at that time then?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just something you did later?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I just had all these papers that I kept.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you put it together?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: And I put it together after I got back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is great.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: It's a scrapbook.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, my goodness. Great.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: See, I started -- I started this scrapbook -- these scrap books here were vacations. This is my honeymoon 1949, and then these were just vacations. Then this is when my first son was born. And then this is when my second son was born, and then there's something from every year.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's like a history of the area.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's incredible.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: You can look at this and look it over, and see if there's anything you have any questions about. I'll try to answer it as much I can. (END OF REAL PLAYER PART ONE; BEGIN REAL PLAYER PART TWO.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now this is great. "Coeds tears flow when soldiers leave." (Laughter.) I'll bet. Spend a lot of time with the coeds there?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I've spent some time, not too just coeds at Bradley. Just some girls from town, Peoria. You know, we had -- had a little girl that worked in a drug store, just around the corner from the campus that I dated when I was there. And there was a family in Peoria who -- the woman was a sister to Fibber McGee. Do you remember Fibber McGee and Molly on the radio?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: The woman was a sister to Fibber McGee and that family sort of took me in there, and I would go have Sunday dinner at their house, and they were very good to me. Carter -- Carter was the family name and we exchanged cards and letters for years after that, but then they eventually passed away.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So Fibber didn't ever come by, uh?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. Yeah. Yeah, my claim -- my claim to fame -- of course, when I was in the -- when I was down in Bradley Polytech Institution, Lou Grosser was in B unit. I was in the A unit, and I played basketball with Lou Grosser. And then when I got out of the service, I played softball with Don Chihuly. He played center field and I played left field on the same team.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's my flag.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Is that Shemya?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, sure is.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Island of Shemya. Little islands.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So this is one of the Aleutian Islands?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Closer to Alaska or farther out?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Father out. It was -- it was either the farthest or the next to the farthest island out in the Aleutian chain. There was still a --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you're getting close to it.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. 400 miles from the Russian Creole Island.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess you said that. These are great scrapbooks. I suppose I have all this stuff laying around just not in scrapbooks.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: We had a big runway. This was all runway along there. And I lived up here in the end of the island someplace.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mostly B-24s there?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Boxcars, flying boxcars, yeah, and like I said, they got the B-29s came in and just right near the end of war. Here's our first B-29.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Too darn much wind on Shemya.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: It was windy. It was windy. It was nasty. The weather was nasty all time. It was -- in that weatherwise it might have been a little depressing, but.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any casualties to deal with there?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Probably more from accidents then?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. We had -- we had some deaths there, but no casualties.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nothing from enemy fire?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No, nothing from enemy fire. We had a number of plane crashes, but the planes always crashed on the next island because the next island had a mountain on it. And they would. We had few plane crashes on Shemya. If you run off the runway and that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Who did these drawings?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Somebody up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Somebody from the camp?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: There's a guy, Bill Maudlin, did a lot of the drawings. And then Al Capp, was it? Not Al Capp.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Sure. That's the guy that did Lem and Abner.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Li'l Abner.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did I say?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Lem and Abner.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's different. We used to carry Lem and Abner on the radio station I worked at.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I remember Lem and Abner. Little five watt someplace.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Li'l Abner.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's the ship I came on, Carl Schurz.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: "1,022 brides and G.I. juniors due in U.S." That's the war brides and the children of war brides coming in. Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I don't remember all these things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. SNAFU. I know what SNAFU is. What's this? TARFU?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: TARFU. Things are really fucked up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: SUSFU?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I don't remember that one. There was -- there was. I don't remember all, but they were all the same thing, SCUF. We had situation all fucked up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, that's the one I've always heard.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Things are really fucked up. I can't remember the other ones. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've never seen those before. Now I'm going to have to figure out what they mean. There we go. There's Shemya. Yeah, that's way out there.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's just a little tiny island.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, my goodness.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That too was father than Shemya. That was there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, yeah, I'm sure there was no problem with the B-29s, right?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: These are Creoles right there that we bombed and this of course was Japan right there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess that's -- what were they going to do once they got to Alaska, if they succeeded?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fight their way through Canada, I guess.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: There's the corporal with the crutch.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's the corporal with the crutch. I have one ever of these crutches. I wasn't quite sure. This is not my dad's. I got one later. The only thing my dad had was the PFC stripes. I think he still has. I think they ended up raising his rank to T-5 after he got back to the States before he was actually discharged.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: That's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, that's very good. I'd say you've got a wonderful personal history.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Do you want to look at these? They're kind of decrepit, they're falling apart. Those are just -- those are people I hang out with.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Hung around with.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This must be during training?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. This is Camp Grant.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There we go, Camp Grant, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Illinois. Basic training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have a camera? Were you taking all of these pictures yourself?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah, I had a camera. I don't remember taking these pictures, but when I was up in the Aleutian Islands, I had a camera, and we had our own -- we developed our own pictures, too. We had a little dark room. We did our own developing. My grandfather, he lived to be 105 years old.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's great. Was he in World War I or no?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that Spanish American or?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: He wasn't in any wars. He wasn't in any wars.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: My grandfather was in World War I. Well, if he lived to be 105, when was he born?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, God. When did he die? I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It sounds like almost he would have been born before the Civil War?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No, I can't remember. I'd have to look back at my scrapbook --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, no. Don't worry.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: -- to see when he died.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm just curious. Anchorage, Alaska. These, boy, these are fantastic. This is a postcard, this Anchorage, Alaska thing?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I think that's a picture.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It's got the little writing on it. Here is what it looks like.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I don't know. It may be a postcard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Spring training. Playing baseball in the snow.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Crazy things. This is the letter I wrote on the train going from Camp Reynolds, Pennsylvania to Prince Rupert, Canada and up to Whittier. October I went up there. I went to Canada in October. I think I said November.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I just can't imagine that. I would think you would have been dealing with a lot of depression and cabin fever.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: They used to have on Attu, when we were in those tents, they'd have what they call willy watts. They were when the wind would blow 60 miles an hour and then you'd get dead calm. And then the wind would blow at 60 miles an hour and you'd get dead calm. The wind would come down off the mountains. It was strange because.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long of a break between?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Oh, maybe ten minutes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. Well, that would drive you nuts. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: It would drive you nuts. This is Hartman. I remember him. He played the guitar. He's the guy that played the guitar.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that a dog you had up there?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Well, that's a dog we put up in the bed one time. It wasn't our dog. We just went ahead and took a picture. I did have a dog later on when I was down at the station house hospital, I had a husky. There's my accordion.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There you go. Flatbush Flanagan.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: This is interesting. That's an outhouse. Shit house number one. (Laughter.) Harold Roberts, he was from Titusville, Pennsylvania. He and I bummed around together up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've spent some time in Titusville. The person I talked to was from Franklin, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Uh-huh. Probably nothing there. I was airplane crazy. Always had been.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you originally want to get into the Army Air Force?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Well, I really wanted to get in the navy. But no, I didn't think I'd ever qualify for the Army Air Force. There was one plane crash we had a B-38. That's real bad. These were scrap airplanes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: We had a lot of scrap airplanes up there, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was a B-25.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Russian graves?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They had these long posts for the graves?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Apparently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because of the snow so they'd have a marker, I guess.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Apparently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow. Boy, these are really amazing.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Now there's when we -- when we went to go out our door one time and we were snowed in, we had to dig our way out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. Couldn't really be claustrophobic there, could you?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: No. Like I said I somehow survived it. There's one of our Saturday night parties. We used to get together every Saturday night when I was in the station hospital. Every Saturday night we had a party in somebody's hut. And we used to drink ethyl alcohol.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Yeah. We'd cut it with various things. It was pretty hard to drink straight. There's my dog.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There you go. Pretty good.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: I've got to do something about this. This is really falling apart.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, but the pictures are still in great shape.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: Whoops. I'm sorry. I did that. This is all just junk. These are buddies I got to see when I got back home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. That's very good.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Farren
sp.p: They're old, they're old.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Like I said I think I've got boxes of pictures I'd love to find some time to do something like that with those.
(THE END OF THE INTERVIEW)
